title: I Worked at LinkedIn. Stop Making These Profile Mistakes
summary: Part two of the LinkedIn Masterclass: Cherie (ex-LinkedIn profile team, teaches a LinkedIn class at Stanford GSB) and Jean review three listener-submitted profiles, covering headline length, profile photo best practices from LinkedIn's own click research, banners, the name-pronunciation feature, using volunteer sections when you lack work experience, and making long About sections scannable. They close with 'LinkedIn Lunatics' examples of 'broetry' and hustle-culture posts, arguing every post should aim to deliver value and teach something.

ideas.idea: Your headline is prime real estate and should carry two or three ideas at most, not a six-item sentence, so people can grok what you are about instantly.
ideas.detail: A submitted profile strung together scholar, marketing, community builder, scholarship help and 'engaging and connecting people wherever I land'; the hosts advise cutting generic lines that could describe a million people.

ideas.idea: Every empty section of a LinkedIn profile is unused real estate; the banner in particular is underutilized and can show you as a leader.
ideas.detail: One submitter filled her banner with photos of herself speaking at a podium and receiving awards plus keywords 'scholar, connector, activator', which the hosts said made her look like a leader at first glance.

ideas.idea: Use the name-pronunciation recording feature, and if you are 'extra', pack a greeting and call to action into those ten seconds.
ideas.detail: Cherie's recording says 'Hello, welcome to my profile... I'm a podcast host and startup co-founder. Follow me to learn more about venture capital, media, startups and technology', which she calls a black-diamond tactic that takes five seconds to record.

ideas.idea: Listing your current top university and a co-founder title in the headline is an effective information shortcut, but drop awards nobody outside your niche recognizes.
ideas.detail: For a Stanford student's headline 'Stanford University, co-founder at X, Diana Award 2024', the hosts liked the first two and questioned the award since readers have no context.

ideas.idea: An About section containing only an email address is better than nothing because it is a call to action, but one dialed first-person sentence about your mission would 10x the profile.
ideas.detail: Advice to the student founder: say what your company and award are about and what you care about, following the beginner formula from part one.

ideas.idea: Students and early-career people should fill their profiles with volunteering, publications and honors, and even babysitting belongs on LinkedIn because it shows responsibility.
ideas.detail: The hosts praise a college student for using the volunteer, publication and honors sections and say putting what you have beats leaving it blank.

ideas.idea: Have a public profile photo where you are smiling, looking directly at the camera, and with your body facing toward the profile text, because LinkedIn's research found those get the most clicks.
ideas.detail: Insider knowledge from the profile team; some people have no photo or restrict who can see it, which hurts discoverability. Cherie admits she has ignored the advice for an artistic looking-away photo.

ideas.idea: A headline that pairs a credential with a mission, like 'CFP financial planner helping first-generation wealth builders', gives credibility and purpose in one line.
ideas.detail: The hosts hold up this submitted headline as concise and clear even without knowing what CFP stands for.

ideas.idea: If your About is long, break it into sections with subtitles, shorter paragraphs, bullets or strategic emojis so readers are pulled from one part to the next.
ideas.detail: One submission ran eight paragraphs; Cherie's own profile uses a 'fun facts' subtitle to guide the eye.

ideas.idea: Numbers pop out of dense text and pull the reader's eye through, so include quantitative figures when writing a lot.
ideas.detail: Jean noticed her eyes went straight to '80+ high net worth households' and '124 trillion' in a text-heavy About even before understanding them.

ideas.idea: Remove the third-person opening paragraph that reads like LinkedIn's AI generator; it merely summarizes experience visible elsewhere and weakens a strong first-person profile.
ideas.detail: Cherie recognized the standard AI-generated tone immediately and says the profile is stronger without it; stick to first person throughout.

ideas.idea: Even in traditional industries like banking, consulting or the military, your profile should show personality; the more you stand out to the reader, the better.
ideas.detail: Cherie pushes back on 'I'm professional and don't want any personality', comparing LinkedIn to the interests section of a printed resume.

ideas.idea: Avoid 'broetry', the one-line-per-sentence bragging style that LinkedIn staff actually named, because it reads as AI-written and insufferable.
ideas.detail: Example from the LinkedIn Lunatics subreddit: 'I stayed up for 72 hours straight... I hit a new gear I never thought possible'; commenters noted 72 hours awake is when you go to the ER.

ideas.idea: Stop promoting hustle culture and hyperbole on LinkedIn; honest conversation about the realities of building a startup is more valuable.
ideas.detail: A post bragging about taking three days of maternity leave ('CEOs and CTOs, your code is your baby') prompted the hosts to say such content is unhealthy for the discourse.

ideas.idea: Relating a personal-life lesson to work can be a great window into who you are, but only if done tactfully and not as a bald lead-in to an empty lesson.
ideas.detail: The 'I had a baby, here's what it taught me about B2B' post is the failure mode; done well, the same move shows the personal side alongside the professional.

ideas.idea: The leading principle for any LinkedIn post is to deliver value: ask what you can teach and what insight about your industry or career others would benefit from.
ideas.detail: If your posts are not engaging, or you are scared to start, reframe around teaching rather than bragging or one-upping; the hosts say that content belongs on X/Twitter and want LinkedIn to be a place people learn from each other.
